h: Ambedkar and Phule under watch: from an anonymous tweet to the PMO
dek: An anonymous X post called anti-caste readings 'poison', and within days the Education Ministry was asking universities to account for these courses.
body: An unnamed account on X wrote that everything being taught, from patriarchy to the annihilation of caste and the critique of Manu, was filling young minds with poison, and that a 'leftist gang' was behind it. Posts like this appear every day. The difference was that this time the echo reached the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).

According to Scroll's report, at the end of September an Education Ministry official cited information received from the PMO and asked university departments for an 'urgent' reply: comment on these courses and say how many students are studying them. The targets are readings by writers such as Ambedkar, Periyar, Savitribai Phule and Gail Omvedt, who link caste and patriarchy to control over education, land, temple entry and knowledge.

Several teachers at Delhi University and JNU, including N Sukumar, R Mahalakshmi and Ajay Gudavarthy, see this as direct political interference in teaching. Their question is why the government should examine a syllabus on the complaint of an unknown account, and on the strength of what expertise.

The Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association says that if you disagree with ideas, debate them; don't get files opened. Teachers fear that caution will now replace curiosity in the classroom, and the habit of obeying orders will replace dissent. When every course and every student is counted and sent upwards, both those who teach and those who learn come under surveillance.

Interestingly, demand for Dalit studies courses has grown, and some classes have more than a hundred students. One scholar guesses that pleasing upper castes angry over the UGC's anti-discrimination rules, which came this year, may also lie behind this move.
nazar: Ambedkar's name is spoken with respect in Parliament, while his books are coming under suspicion in the classroom. This double standard sends a clear message to Dalit, Bahujan and Adivasi students that even reading their own history is now a risky business.
If the noise of social media starts taking the shape of government orders, it weakens not only the freedom of universities but also the Constitution's idea of equality.
sawal: Is teaching questions about caste the poison, or is caste itself?
ref: Gail Omvedt
An American-born sociologist who became an Indian citizen. She wrote important books on the Phule-Ambedkar tradition, the Dalit movement and farmers' movements.
UGC anti-discrimination rules
Rules of the University Grants Commission meant to stop discrimination on campus on the basis of caste and other grounds, and to set up a system for complaints.
ank: students in some Dalit studies classes

h: Officials versus the Assembly in Kashmir: the real price of Union Territory status
dek: Two senior officials wrote to the Speaker against a resolution to restore statehood, raising the question of how far an elected government's word counts in Jammu and Kashmir.
body: On 28 September the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly passed a resolution demanding the restoration of statehood. Later Chief Minister Omar Abdullah revealed that Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo and Law Secretary Achal Sethi had written separate letters to Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather saying the resolution should not be taken up, because the matter was before the Supreme Court.

Abdullah was most surprised by the Law Secretary, who by the rules works under him, yet gave an opinion against the Chief Minister's resolution without telling him. He said this is possible only in a Union Territory. A former law secretary also agreed that nothing like this ever happened when it was a state.

Safwat Zargar's report traces the root to 2019, when the state was broken up and made a Union Territory. Officials now answer to both the Lieutenant Governor and the Chief Minister, and the business rules that divide powers between the two have still not been made. Legislators have complained since 2019 that the bureaucracy does not give importance to elected representatives.

Legal expert Sheikh Showkat Hussain points out that the Assembly is master of its own proceedings and the executive cannot interfere in them. The High Court and the Supreme Court have also expressed displeasure in the past at the stubborn attitude of officials here.

Every party except the BJP condemned this interference. The BJP instead demanded the Speaker's resignation. A privilege motion by PDP legislator Waheed Para has been sent to a committee, but the National Conference government has so far taken no action against the officials.
nazar: The people of Jammu and Kashmir turned out in huge numbers in 2024 to elect their government. If that government's own officer stands in the way of the Assembly, this is not just an administrative tangle; it is an insult to democracy and to the federal structure.
The longer the promise of restoring statehood hangs, the deeper Kashmiris' feeling will grow that their voice is at the mercy of officials in Delhi.
sawal: Who stands above an elected Assembly?
ref: Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019

With the removal of Article 370, this law split the state into two Union Territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. Jammu and Kashmir got an Assembly, but major powers stayed with the Lieutenant Governor.
Privilege motion
Legislators bring this motion when someone is accused of violating the rights of the House or its members. The matter goes to the privileges committee for inquiry.

h: A fifteen-minute meeting could have avoided the street fight
dek: Sanjay K Jha says that if the Chief Election Commissioner had simply met the Opposition, there would have been no police, detentions or confrontation, but the government chose to defend every excess.
body: On 6 October Opposition MPs walked from Parliament House towards Nirvachan Sadan, barely fifteen minutes away on foot. They wanted to meet Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Sanjay K Jha says a short meeting could have avoided the whole confrontation, but the head of the Commission showed no moral courage to face the Opposition.

The writer recalls that when Rahul Gandhi put forward evidence of irregularities in Karnataka's voter lists, the reply was not facts but the label 'anti-national'. In the Form 6 controversy, it emerged from inside the Commission itself that many decisions were taken alone, without the agreement of the commissioners.

The piece also cites Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan's remark that a process which shuts lakhs and crores of citizens out of the right to vote is arbitrary in itself. According to Jha, at such a time the Prime Minister should have stepped in to restore trust, but instead he defended every wrong step.

Instead of answering complaints from Bengal, Haryana and Maharashtra, the BJP changed the subject by listing examples from other states. Since 2 October students, activists and citizens' groups have been on the streets, and they are not getting permission even for Jantar Mantar, though peaceful assembly is a right given by the Constitution.
The writer concludes that when institutions run from accountability, protest becomes a citizen's constitutional duty. The confrontation was created not by the Opposition but by the refusal to talk.
nazar: Names being struck off voter lists hit the poor, migrant workers, Muslims and people on the margins first, since they have the least power to gather documents. The Commission avoiding dialogue at such a time means silencing exactly their voices.
In a democracy, if the umpire starts fearing a meeting with the players, it is hard for trust in the game to hold.
sawal: How can we trust a Commission that is afraid to meet the Opposition?
ref: Form 6
The form for adding a new name to the voter list. Changes made to it are disputed, and the Supreme Court has said it did not approve the altered form.
Nirvachan Sadan
The headquarters of the Election Commission of India in Delhi, on Ashoka Road, a short distance from Parliament House.

h: Himalayan lakes can be seen growing, but the warning never arrives
dek: Sikkim's South Lhonak disaster shows that the danger of glacial lakes is not unseen, just unheard.
body: On the night of 3 October 2023 a huge mass of rock and ice fell into South Lhonak lake in Sikkim. A wave about twenty metres high rose, the lake's wall of debris broke, and nearly five crore (50 million) cubic metres of water poured into the Teesta. At least 55 people died, eighty thousand people in four districts were affected, and the 1200 megawatt Teesta-III dam at Chungthang was washed away.

The writer says this disaster was not sudden. Scientists had been watching the lake for years and pipes had even been installed on it. Still, the warning that mattered most did not reach the people who needed it in time. The river gauges downstream were the first things swept away, and the first news came not from a machine but from an ITBP post stationed eight kilometres below the lake.

Bose points out that today the European Union's Copernicus satellites take free images of the Himalayas every few days. Anyone can open a browser and see how much a lake is spreading year after year. Nepal's Tsho Rolpa lake was a small pond in the 1950s; now it is larger than one and a half square kilometres.

The danger does not respect borders. Of the 47 dangerous lakes identified in a 2020 ICIMOD study, 42 are in the Kosi basin, whose water flows into Bihar. The Green Climate Fund has given money to drain only four of Nepal's lakes. In India the NDMA started a Rs 150 crore programme in 2024, but the stress is more on surveys and less on warnings.

The writer suggests three direct steps: dated lake reports in plain language from satellite data that reach the district officer's phone; work beyond the four lakes, and honest conversation with the villages that are waiting; and real-time sharing of river data between India and Nepal.
nazar: In mountain disasters the first to drown are those who live in the valleys, by the rivers and below the dams: workers, farmers and residents of small towns. When the technology is free and the news still does not arrive, this is a failure not of nature but of governance.
For people in Bihar's Kosi region, this question is not about Nepal; it is about their own homes.
sawal: If the danger can be seen from a satellite, why does it not reach the village?
ref: Glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)
When a lake held behind a wall of debris in front of a melting glacier suddenly bursts, a terrible flood hits the valley below. In the Himalayas this danger is growing as temperatures rise.
ICIMOD
An intergovernmental body based in Kathmandu that does research on mountains, glaciers and water for the eight countries of the Hindu Kush Himalaya.

h: The middle class that took off with liberalisation has now stalled
dek: Writing from Delhi, Jawed Naqvi says India's market-driven growth made those at the top rich and left those in the middle restless.
body: Dawn's Delhi correspondent Jawed Naqvi says that the new middle class born of Manmohan Singh's economic reforms in 1991 later prepared the ground for Narendra Modi's rise. He describes this class as two-faced: at times it dreams of becoming rich, and at times it fears the insecurity of a labourer.

Riding on the reforms and the IT industry, this class grew from a few lakh to crores. But according to the writer, its growth stopped after 2014. Prices climbed, salaries stalled, and growth became 'K'-shaped, with those at the top going up and the rest sliding down. The protests by young people and students in recent months are a sign of this disillusionment.

The pandemic widened the gap. Citing a 2021 Oxfam report, he says the wealth of Indian billionaires grew by 35 percent during the lockdown, while crores of people lost their livelihoods. Even a suggestion of a modest wealth tax on the richest families was never acted on.

Naqvi compares this with China, where the government is reining in big tech companies and real estate tycoons in the name of 'common prosperity'. He sees in this Nehru's idea that big industry should stay in the hands of the state and wealth should not pile up in a few hands. Indira Gandhi's nationalisation of banks was on the same path, while later governments opened the doors to private capital.
In the end he puts a question to middle-class protesters: in a country counted among the world's big economies, why do eighty crore (800 million) people depend on free rations?
nazar: Middle-class anger often stays limited to its own EMIs and jobs. The writer has a point: until this anger connects with the eighty crore people standing in the ration queue, no movement will reach the root of inequality.
No model of growth that leaves out workers, farmers and the informal sector can last.
sawal: Will the anger of the middle class reach the ration queue or not?
ref: K-shaped recovery
A recovery after an economic crisis in which the rich and big companies bounce back quickly, while the poor and small businesses sink further.
Common Prosperity
A slogan and policy of the Chinese government that speaks of narrowing the income gap by curbing extreme wealth and the monopolies of big companies.
photo_note: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte

h: Teach men instead of shrinking women
dek: Kanwal Singh argues that in the name of protection we made women's world smaller, when it was men's behaviour that needed to change.
body: On paper, women in India have the same rights as men, but on the street, in the market and on the bus they cannot move about with the same freedom and ease. Kanwal Singh says our whole arrangement is upside down: restrictions are placed on women, on when they go out, what they wear and whom they go with, when the question should be about men's behaviour.

According to her, sexual violence does not fall suddenly from the sky. Staring, crude jokes, stalking: these small things together create a climate in which a woman is uneasy everywhere. Now all of this is happening online too, where women who speak on social issues face threats and trolling.

Laws became stricter after the Nirbhaya case of 2012, but the writer believes the cycle of violence has not stopped. Linking a woman's body with shame also affects health: many women delay going to the doctor, and serious illnesses are caught late.

Inequality begins at home, where there are different rules for sons and daughters and housework is not shared equally. Schools teach discipline, but there are no serious lessons on consent and accountability. Women make up 13.6 percent of Parliament and about 9 percent of state assemblies, so their voice is also weak in planning safe public spaces.
The writer's solution is simple: men should call out other men's sexism, families should question the restrictions placed on daughters, and women should lead in making policy.
nazar: This applies to women of every class, but the heaviest burden falls on those who travel alone to work every day: domestic workers, labourers, nurses, students. For them, restriction means losing livelihood and education.
The real measure of safety is how freely a woman can step outside, not how often she is advised to stay at home.
sawal: Why are the restrictions always on the daughter, and never on the son?
ref: Nirbhaya case
The gang rape and death of a young woman on a bus in Delhi in December 2012. Protests followed across the country, and rape laws were changed in 2013.

h: Democracy decided on the phone screen before the vote
dek: Election campaigning has stepped down from the rally stage and settled quietly into every voter's phone, and the weakest voter is the easiest target.
body: Kumar Saikrishna Nayak, a history student at Delhi University, says that electoral persuasion no longer speaks loudly to a crowd; instead it whispers separately into each person's ear. This happens not at rallies but in smartphone feeds, where data models decide who is shown what, and when.

According to the writer, its biggest trick is that voters feel they formed their opinions themselves. The videos or posts that appear seem to have come on their own, when in fact they are messages tested in advance. Two people from the same neighbourhood, in the same circumstances, can live in completely different worlds of news.

He explains that even before people reach the polling booth, it has already been tested which message will work on whom. Predictive models and targeted ads in the United States, state-controlled algorithms in China, and the European Union's rules on political advertising in force since October 2025 are all different pictures of the same change.

The writer's most important point is that this technology does not treat all citizens the same way. Those with less digital understanding, fewer other sources of news, or whose social standing does not give them the confidence to question what they see on the screen, are the easiest prey for this silent campaigning.

As a solution he calls for transparency in political ads, a ban on fine-grained targeting based on behaviour, and independent scrutiny of campaign data. He also tells voters to be most suspicious of whatever feels most comfortable.
nazar: In India, those with the least social capital mostly come from Dalit, Adivasi, backward and poor communities. If the campaign machine targets exactly their weakness, the equal promise of one person, one vote is hollowed out from within.
The Election Commission will have to watch not just the booth but also the feed.
sawal: Is your opinion really yours, or your feed's?
ref: Microtargeting
A method of dividing people into small groups using data on their online behaviour, and showing each group a different political message.
Cambridge Analytica
A British data company accused in 2018 of using the data of crores of Facebook users in election campaigns without permission. It later shut down.

h: Rising heat has now reached the womb and the newborn
dek: A survey of a thousand doctors and nurses in five countries shows that heatwaves are becoming a new danger for pregnant women and newborns.
body: The Wellcome foundation spoke to a thousand health workers who care for mothers and babies in India, Australia, Brazil, Britain and Zimbabwe, two hundred of them from India. According to the report, 73 percent said cases of pregnant women with heat-related problems had risen over the past five years, and 76 percent saw a growing effect on the health of babies in the womb or newborns.

Almost all of them said they had treated women and children badly affected by heatwaves. More than a third saw low birth weight babies and stunted growth in the womb, as many saw dehydration and illness in newborns, and about a third recorded difficulties with feeding, breathing and controlling body temperature.

The difficulty is not only physical but also about access. More than one in four health workers said women could not even reach the hospital because of the intense heat, and nearly thirty percent saw a rise in emergency cases.

The report also recalls older research: every one degree rise in temperature increases the risk of premature birth by about five percent, and complications linked to childbirth are nearly a quarter higher during heatwaves.

Wellcome's demand is that countries' climate and health plans give a separate place to pregnant women and newborns, that the World Health Organization draw up clear treatment guidelines on heat and pregnancy, and that heatwave data be added to monitoring. 81 percent of those surveyed fear that if nothing is done, things will get worse.
nazar: In India this danger falls hardest on women who work in fields, brick kilns and construction sites until the last months of pregnancy, whose homes have tin roofs and whose hospitals are miles away. Our plans to deal with heatwaves still barely mention the pregnant woman worker.
Talk of climate justice is incomplete until it includes the health of mothers and newborns.
sawal: On heatwave days, who will give the pregnant woman worker leave?
ref: Wellcome
A large independent charitable trust based in London that funds research in health and science, especially on the link between climate and health.
Heat Action Plan
Plans made by states and cities to reduce deaths and illness from heatwaves. In India this began in Ahmedabad in 2013.

h: Women got seats in Parliament, but men still hold the keys to decisions
dek: A Pakistani climate policy analyst says increasing the number of women will achieve nothing until real authority comes into their hands.
body: Ayesha Khan argues that empowering women in Pakistan is not just a matter of justice but a condition for the country's progress. A country of more than twenty-four crore (240 million) people is simply wasting a large part of the ability of half its population.

It starts with education. Literacy in the country is 63 percent, but 73 percent among men and only 54 percent among women. Among rural women the figure is stuck at 44 percent. A woman who cannot read can neither understand an agreement nor benefit from a government scheme.

The gap in work is even bigger. Men's labour force participation is 80 percent, women's 24 percent. Of the women who do work, nearly three quarters are in insecure jobs, mostly in farming. On top of that, almost all the unpaid work of the home and care falls on them, eating up their time, education and chances to get ahead.

The writer says presence and power are not the same thing. Women hold about 22 percent of the seats in the National Assembly, but only around five and a quarter percent of federal government jobs, and they are almost absent from the top posts in the police, the law and the army.

The climate crisis makes this gap even more dangerous. Women manage water and food, but they have no voice in meetings on disaster preparedness and budgets. The writer wants success to be measured not by enrolments and seats, but by how many women really hold decisions on budgets, departments, businesses and the household in their own hands.
nazar: This picture is not unfamiliar on this side of the border either. India too has passed a women's reservation law, but the custom of the 'pradhan pati' (the husband who runs the village council in place of his elected wife) in panchayats shows how wide the gap is between the seat and the authority.
Until the woman who toils in the field is part of decisions on land, loans and water, the fight against climate change will stay incomplete.
sawal: When will the woman in the chair get the key?
ref: Labour force participation rate
The share of the working-age population that is in a job or work, or looking for work. It shows how many people are active in the economy.
Unpaid care work

Work such as cooking, looking after children and the elderly, and fetching water and fuel, for which no wage is paid. It is not counted in GDP, but neither the home nor the economy can run without it.

h: Gaza's wound: how can there be healing where the war never stops?
dek: Gaza writer Saeed Alsaloul explains that in an unending war, even beginning to heal the wounds of the mind is impossible.
body: After three years of war, the death toll in Gaza has passed 74,000, and more than 1,400 people have been killed even after the ceasefire of October 2025. Saeed Alsaloul says that in this situation, talking about recovering from trauma is itself meaningless, because trauma is not a past event but part of every day.

The writer tells his own story. In the first two months of the war, bombs fell on six houses around him and sixty neighbours were killed. His own home was damaged, and his mother, his sister and he himself were injured. He found the body of his eight-year-old student Mohammed in the rubble. Many relatives and friends are gone, and according to him it was often the kindest and most promising who went.

Figures from the United Nations Population Fund show that more than ten lakh (one million) children need psychological help, and 96 percent of them feel that death is near. According to studies, 61 percent of young people have PTSD, and about 88 percent of adults show its symptoms. Things were bad even before the war: by 2022, 71 percent of adults were depressed.

The writer's body records this fear too. His chest tightens at the sound of a drone, his hands shake at the sound of gunfire, he cannot concentrate, and he rarely smiles. The guilt of having survived deepens the wound further.

He writes that stories no longer touch him; he reads to forget. Stories of human courage fall short before the reality of Gaza, because the world's indifference itself seems stranger than any fiction.
nazar: A ceasefire may exist on paper, but there is no peace in a society whose children wait for death every moment. Mental health must be treated as the first need in relief work, not the last.
India has long raised its voice for Palestine. What is needed today is for that voice to turn into a concrete demand for the treatment and recovery of Gaza's children.
sawal: Where the fear never ends, how can healing begin?
ref: PTSD
Post-traumatic stress disorder. A condition of fear, anxiety and nightmares that lasts a long time after a terrible event.
United Nations Population Fund
UNFPA, the United Nations agency that works on reproductive health and the well-being of women and young people.

h: Cyber patrols in every region, in the name of fake news
dek: Pakistan's cyber investigation agency has announced a crackdown on 'anti-state propaganda', and Dawn asks whether the real target is false news or dissent.
body: Ali Nasir Rizvi, the new head of Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), has announced a zero-tolerance policy against fake news and anti-state propaganda. 'Cyber patrolling units' have been set up in every region for this.

Dawn's editorial first objects to the words. Neither fake news nor anti-state propaganda has a clear legal definition. When the crime itself is vague, the right to decide passes to whoever holds the stick.

The paper accepts that the agency also has a legitimate job. Protecting people from online fraud, harassment and financial crimes is necessary, and it recently acted against fraudulent call centres. But questions remain about the patrol units: whom will they watch, under what law, who will keep an eye on them, and how will ordinary citizens be protected from excess?

The timing also raises suspicion. A recent amendment to the PECA law has already made spreading 'false information' a crime, which journalists and human rights groups strongly opposed. Meanwhile the government and the opposition are at loggerheads over protests. In such a climate, the editorial feels the real target is dissent, not misinformation.

The paper suggests that the answer to false news is not prosecution and surveillance but credible government communication, media literacy among people, and accountability for platforms. Trust is not built with a legal stick.
nazar: For India this story is like a mirror. Here too, action has been taken against posts by journalists and ordinary people using fact-check units, IT rules and vague charges like sedition.
On both sides of the border, the biggest price for the way governments fight 'fake news' is paid by those who have no means other than their voice.
sawal: Who will decide what is a lie, when even telling the truth becomes a crime?
ref: PECA
Pakistan's cyber law, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016. Journalists' organisations allege that recent amendments are being used to criminalise online criticism.
NCCIA
Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency, given responsibility for investigating cyber crimes after this was separated from the FIA.

h: A new offensive in Yemen: winning ground is not enough, unity is needed
dek: Abdullah Bandar Al-Otaibi argues that the Yemeni government's gains will not last unless the divisions in the anti-Houthi camp are overcome.
body: Yemen's government has launched a new counter-offensive against the Houthis and has taken back some areas on the Red Sea coast near Bab al-Mandab. A hundred fighter jets of the Saudi-led coalition are flying day and night, and the Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi soil. This is the biggest fighting since the 2022 United Nations ceasefire.

According to the writer, the real battleground is the western coast. Iran has disrupted the route through Hormuz, so Gulf oil now goes through the Red Sea, and control of Bab al-Mandab decides power across the whole region. The second key front is Taiz, which links the north, the south and the coast. The fighting on several sides in Marib aims to wear the Houthis down.

But the biggest weakness lies on the government's own side. In the anti-Houthi camp, Tareq Saleh's National Resistance, the Southern Giants Brigades and units linked to the Islah party all act separately, while the Houthis' political and military command comes from one place.

The writer lists four tests of success: holding the coast and the islands of the strait, opening the Taiz-Aden road, forcing the Houthis to pull their forces back from Taiz, and bringing a single command, salaries and basic services to the areas won. The Houthis' decisions are also tied to bargaining between Tehran and Washington.

Ordinary people are being crushed in the middle of all this. According to the World Health Organization, more than five thousand people have been killed or injured since August, two lakh (200,000) have been displaced and cholera cases have tripled.
nazar: This piece is about war strategy, but its final figures tell the real story. In Yemen's war, amid outside powers' calculations about oil and routes, the country's poor are homeless, sick and hungry.

Much of India's trade passes through the Red Sea, and the livelihoods of lakhs of Indians working in the Gulf are tied to it. India should be a voice here not for an arms race but for ceasefire and relief.
sawal: Whose victory is it, when only cholera and hunger are advancing?
ref: Bab al-Mandab
The narrow sea passage between Yemen and Djibouti in Africa that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. A key link in the world's oil trade.
Houthis
An armed movement from northern Yemen that captured the capital Sanaa in 2014. It has Iran's support.

h: Young people of sinking islands: a bridge from the Pacific to the Caribbean
dek: A Global Voices piece describes how young people in Oceania and the Caribbean are building a shared path, rooted in local leadership, to fight the climate crisis.
by: Adele Roeder, Orit Novak, Chelsea Adams and Zahiris P. Francisco
body: Small island nations account for less than one percent of the world's total emissions, yet they bear the sharpest blows of the climate crisis. In these Caribbean countries, 65 percent of the population lives on low-lying land by the sea, and internal displacement there has grown sixfold in recent years.

The piece begins with the difference between Australia and these islands. Australia is relatively safe, though even there more than 23 percent of homeless people are under twenty-five. In Fiji and the Caribbean, the climate crisis is an everyday disaster.

The writers talk about unfinished work. Many development projects are left halfway, water supply and infrastructure remain incomplete, and people face the next storm with the same gaps. Fijian community leader John Whippy and Dominican Republic activist and journalist Zahiris Francisco bring these experiences forward.

The piece sharply criticises voluntourism, in which about one crore (10 million) people a year travel in the name of service. According to the writers, it repeats old colonial relationships, where outsiders decide what local people need.

The alternative is the Oceania Caribbean Climate Alliance, which connects young people in Brisbane and Castries, the capital of Saint Lucia. The network is preparing for a youth climate conference in Saint Lucia in December 2027. The message is clear: taking action matters, and backing local leadership matters just as much.
nazar: India's Sundarbans, Lakshadweep and coastal fishing settlements face the same danger. Here too, plans are often made from outside and left unfinished.
Direct ties among young people of the Global South, without depending on the goodwill of rich countries, can give new strength to the fight for climate justice.
sawal: Those who come in the name of help, whom do they really come for?
ref: Small Island Developing States
SIDS, a group of small island countries in the Pacific, the Caribbean and the Indian Ocean, most at risk from rising sea levels.
Voluntourism
A mix of volunteering and tourism in which people go to poor countries for a few days to do service. Critics see it as showy and cut off from local needs.

h: Calling Sahil's death a suicide is not enough
dek: Kailash Wankhede's essay reads the death of IIT Bombay student Sahil as a death made by the institution.
body: Fiction writer Kailash Wankhede's essay begins with the story of Sahil, a BTech student found dead in an IIT Bombay hostel on 18 September. That same day, during an exam, he was accused of cheating with an illegal device, he was sent out of the exam hall, and some teachers gave him so-called counselling. A short while later came the news of his death.

The writer asks several direct questions. How was a student sitting in the front row, in full view of several invigilators, cheating? Why has the full CCTV footage not been released, and why does the clip that was circulated confirm only one story? What was actually said in that counselling?

The essay is sharpest on the institution's attitude. The student was declared guilty on social media even before any inquiry; then, after an uproar, an apology came on 21 September, but no accountability was fixed. A forum of teachers came out in defence of the professor, while it had nothing to say for the dead student. The inquiry committee too is made up of people who appear to stand with the institution.

Sahil's family alleged caste harassment, filed an FIR under the Atrocities Prevention Act and held a hunger strike at Azad Maidan. The writer recalls that Darshan Solanki also died at this same institution earlier, and still nothing changed.

Wankhede concludes that in elite institutions of higher education, caste is not visible but it keeps working. Students who are victims cannot even complain, and in the end the power structure protects its own. Despite the law, there has been no arrest, and no court has stepped in.
nazar: From Rohith Vemula until today, the question each time is the same: how alone are Dalit and Adivasi students on these campuses? As long as the inquiry is done by the very people being questioned, trust is hard to restore. This essay carries out the responsibility of literature that includes recording testimony.
sawal: Who will answer for the death of a student on campus?
ref: Atrocities Prevention Act
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. It provides strict punishment and speedy trial for caste crimes against Dalits and Adivasis.
Darshan Solanki
A Dalit student at IIT Bombay whose death set off a major debate on caste discrimination on campus.

h: Kedarnath Singh's ordinary people, who do not give up
dek: Mukteshwar Nath Tiwary reads the stubbornness and dignity of ordinary people in Kedarnath Singh's poetry.
body: This essay by critic Mukteshwar Nath Tiwary, who teaches Hindi at Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan, reads Kedarnath Singh's poetry in connection with the ground it comes from. He says working people, the poor and those on the margins appear again and again in Kedarnath Singh's work, but the poet neither romanticises them nor turns them into great heroes.

The essay's second thread is imagery, that is, placing things before the reader like a concrete picture. Tiwary goes through several poems. In 'Dekho Us Aadmi Ko' (Look at That Man), a man crosses the same city street a thousand times and still does not tire. In 'Pani Mein Ghire Hue Log' (People Surrounded by Water), people trapped by a flood do not complain; they simply hold on.

In the poem 'Chhata' (Umbrella), the umbrella of a Bengali gentleman met after many years seems to the critic like a shield, behind which a man hides his grief and carries on with daily life. In 'Akal Mein Saras' (Cranes in a Drought), an old father's respect for grain brings out an old understanding of farming.

Tiwary also recalls the characters who appear again and again in Kedarnath Singh's poetry: people who fish all day but go home empty-handed, those who sell surma (kohl) every day, old people battling the cold. These people are silent, but there is a kind of resistance even in their silence.
The essay concludes that Kedarnath Singh looked at ordinary life with full seriousness, and that is what makes his poetry a music of roots. Do read the original essay for the poems.
nazar: Today, when literature too is under pressure from noise and spectacle, returning to Kedarnath Singh reminds us that villages, floods, droughts and daily labour are full subjects for poetry. Seeing people on the margins not with pity but as equals is the real commitment.
sawal: Is holding on in silence also a form of resistance?
ref: Kedarnath Singh
Hindi poet born in 1934 in Chakia village of Ballia district, died in 2018. Honoured with the Sahitya Akademi Award for 'Akal Mein Saras' and the Jnanpith in 2013.

h: Tarabai: a voice for a silent woman of history
dek: Rajaram Bhadu's review of Dipti Kushwaha's long poem 'Ek Stri ka Desh: Tarau' sees it as history written through a woman's eyes.
body: Sammukh has published a full feature on Dipti Kushwaha's work 'Ek Stri ka Desh: Tarau' (A Woman's Country: Tarau), with a review by Rajaram Bhadu, a foreword by fiction writer Priyadarshan and a statement by the poet herself. The book is published by Rudraditya Prakashan and is written as a long, epic-like poem.

Tarau, that is Tarabai, was the queen from Shivaji's family who took charge of the Maratha state after the death of her husband Rajaram, and resisted Aurangzeb's army for years. Later a separate seat of power was set up in Kolhapur. In her long life she also spent several years in captivity.

Bhadu's main argument is that this book is not just an account of history. The poet does not worship Tarabai as an invincible heroine, but sees her as a woman living in the tension between warrior, mother and ruler. Her weaknesses and dilemmas are also part of the poem.
According to the reviewer, the poem tries to capture the experience that court history does not record. In history, women are often present yet silent, and this work enters that very silence.

Bhadu sees it as part of contemporary feminist history-writing, which lifts women from the margins and places them as active figures in politics and culture. Priyadarshan's foreword and the poet's statement also carry this idea forward in their own ways.
nazar: Today, when there is a race to turn history into sagas of nationalist heroes, a book that sees a queen as a human being and not a statue is valuable. Rewriting the place of women in history is also a political act.
sawal: How many women of history are still just footnotes?
ref: Wife of Chhatrapati Rajaram, who after his death became regent of the Maratha state and fought a long war against the Mughals. The separate throne of Kolhapur is linked to her.
